record_type_quote: This study presents a conceptual replication of Birulés et al.’s (2020, Experiment 2) investigation of native and nonnative listeners’ selective attention to a talker’s mouth with the goal of better understanding the potentially modulating role of proficiency in listeners’ reliance on audiovisual speech cues.

targets.authors: Birulés, J., Bosch, L., Pons, F., & Lewkowicz, D. J.
targets.title: Highly proficient L2 speakers still need to attend to a talker’s mouth when processing L2 speech.
targets.evidence_quote: This study presents a conceptual replication of Birulés et al.’s (2020, Experiment 2) investigation of native and nonnative listeners’ selective attention to a talker’s mouth with the goal of better understanding the potentially modulating role of proficiency in listeners’ reliance on audiovisual speech cues.
targets.outcome_quote: Findings from one of the videos replicated results from the original study, showing greater attention to the talker’s mouth among L2 than L1 listeners. In both videos, L2 proficiency modulated attention, with more fixations on the mouth among lower proficiency listeners, an effect predicted but not observed in the original study.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The group effect replicated in one video but not the other, and the proficiency correlation explicitly diverged from the original null finding. General support for the hypothesis is not an overall verdict of agreement with the original results.

reasoning: Title, authors, DOI and complete 16-page article verified. One original paper, Experiment 2, is explicitly re-tested in a new sample.
